scenes.heading: Micro-Partitions, Clustering & Pruning
scenes.narration: Snowflake stores data in micro-partitions, and understanding them reveals how pruning makes queries fast.

scenes.heading: What is a micro-partition?
bullets: Small immutable units of roughly 50 to 500 MB of compressed data.
Created automatically as data loads, with no manual partition management.
Store columnar data plus metadata like min and max per column.
That metadata is exactly what lets Snowflake prune at query time.
scenes.narration: Micro-partitions are small immutable chunks that Snowflake creates automatically as you load data. Each one holds columnar values along with metadata such as the minimum and maximum of every column. This means you never manage partitions by hand, yet the engine always knows what each chunk contains.

scenes.heading: How pruning works
scenes.narration: When a query filters on a column, Snowflake first checks each micro-partition's min and max metadata. Any partition whose range cannot contain matching rows is skipped entirely. As a result the engine reads only the partitions that could possibly satisfy the filter.

scenes.heading: Well-clustered vs poorly-clustered
scenes.narration: When data is well clustered, rows sharing a filter value sit in the same few partitions, so pruning skips almost everything else. When it is poorly clustered, those values are scattered across many partitions and the engine must read most of them. Clustering keys, or automatic clustering, keep large tables organized so pruning stays effective.

scenes.heading: Adding a clustering key
scenes.narration: The ALTER statement defines a clustering key so Snowflake reorganizes the data by date and region over time. The clustering information function then reports how well organized the table currently is. Watching that clustering depth tells you whether pruning will be effective for your typical filters.

scenes.text: Micro-partition metadata drives pruning, and good clustering keeps filter values grouped so queries skip most of the data.
scenes.narration: Pruning is only as good as your clustering, so keep the columns you filter on grouped and Snowflake will read almost nothing extra.
